title: Variables / scope
summary: Scope rules (Global, Function, Block), var vs let vs const, and Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ).

explanation.overview: Scope defines variable access boundaries in JavaScript. JavaScript features Global Scope, Function Scope (created by functions), and Block Scope (created by `{}` blocks with `let` and `const`).

sections.heading: var vs let vs const Comparison
sections.content: `var` is function-scoped and hoisted initialized as `undefined`. `let` and `const` are block-scoped and enter a Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) from scope entry until declaration initialization.
bulletPoints: `var`: Function-scoped, re-declarable, hoisted with undefined.
`let`: Block-scoped, re-assignable, cannot re-declare in same block.
`const`: Block-scoped, immutable variable reference binding.

sections.heading: Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)
sections.content: The TDZ is the period between entering a scope and executing the variable's declaration line. Accessing `let` or `const` in TDZ throws a ReferenceError.
bulletPoints: Prevents accessing variables before explicit declaration.
Eliminates silent undefined variable bugs during execution.

keyTakeaways: Prefer `const` by default, `let` when reassignment is required.
Avoid `var` to prevent scope leakage outside blocks.
Understand TDZ to prevent runtime ReferenceErrors.

codeExamples.title: Block Scope & TDZ Demonstration
codeExamples.description: Comparing var leakage vs let block isolation and TDZ error.

mcqs.question: What error occurs when accessing a `let` variable before its declaration line?
mcqs.explanation: Variables declared with `let` or `const` reside in TDZ until declared; accessing them throws ReferenceError.

mcqs.question: Which keyword creates a function-scoped variable that ignores block boundaries?
mcqs.explanation: `var` is function-scoped or globally-scoped, ignoring block `{}` statements.

mcqs.question: What happens when mutating a property on a `const obj = { a: 1 }`?
mcqs.explanation: `const` prevents reassignment of the binding identifier, but does not make object properties immutable.

mcqs.question: What scope is created for `let` inside a standard `for` loop header?
options: A new block scope instance per iteration
mcqs.explanation: `for (let i = 0)...` creates a fresh block binding for `i` in each loop iteration.

mcqs.question: What is logged by `console.log(a); var a = 10;`?
mcqs.explanation: `var a` is hoisted to top of scope initialized with `undefined`.

title: Objects
summary: Key-value property storage, object methods, property descriptors, Object.freeze vs Object.seal.

explanation.overview: Objects are collection of key-value pairs where keys are strings/symbols and values can be any data type. JS objects support property access, iteration, dynamic keys, and property attribute descriptors.

sections.heading: Object Operations & Utility Methods
sections.content: `Object.keys()`, `Object.values()`, and `Object.entries()` allow iterating properties. `Object.assign()` and spread `{...obj}` perform shallow cloning.
bulletPoints: `Object.keys(obj)`: Returns array of own enumerable string keys.
`Object.entries(obj)`: Returns array of `[key, value]` pairs.
Shallow Copy: Nested objects retain shared references.

sections.heading: Immutability: Freeze vs Seal
sections.content: `Object.freeze()` prevents property addition, deletion, and value modification. `Object.seal()` prevents property addition and deletion but allows updating existing values.
bulletPoints: `Object.freeze()`: Fully immutable shallow lock.
`Object.seal()`: Prevents structure changes, allows value updates.
`Object.defineProperty()`: Configures writable, enumerable, and configurable attributes.

keyTakeaways: Objects use key-value string/symbol mappings.
`Object.freeze` prevents edits; `Object.seal` allows updating existing keys.
Spread and Object.assign produce shallow copies.

codeExamples.title: Object Freeze vs Seal
codeExamples.description: Demonstrating behavior of Object.freeze and Object.seal.

mcqs.question: What does `Object.freeze(obj)` prevent on an object?
options: Adding, deleting, and modifying existing properties
mcqs.explanation: `Object.freeze()` locks shallow object properties against addition, deletion, or re-assignment.

mcqs.question: What is the difference between `Object.seal()` and `Object.freeze()`?
options: Seal allows modifying existing property values; Freeze does not
mcqs.explanation: `Object.seal()` allows reassigning existing properties, but blocks adding or deleting keys.

mcqs.question: What data types can be used as Object property keys in JS?
mcqs.explanation: Object property keys in JS can only be Strings or Symbols (numbers are converted to strings).

mcqs.question: What kind of copy is created by `{ ...originalObj }`?
mcqs.explanation: Spread operator creates a shallow copy; nested object references are shared.

mcqs.question: Which method converts an object into an array of key-value pairs `[[key, val], ...]`?
mcqs.explanation: `Object.entries()` returns array of `[key, value]` arrays.

title: Arrays
summary: Ordered list collections, array mutations, indexing, slice/splice, and ES6+ array methods.

explanation.overview: Arrays in JavaScript are zero-indexed, dynamically-sized list objects. Understanding mutating methods (push, pop, splice) vs non-mutating methods (slice, concat, toSpliced) is essential for state management.

sections.heading: Mutating vs Non-Mutating Methods
sections.content: Mutating methods modify original array in place. Non-mutating methods return a fresh array, which is crucial for React state updates.
bulletPoints: Mutating: `push`, `pop`, `shift`, `unshift`, `splice`, `sort`, `reverse`.
Non-mutating: `slice`, `concat`, `map`, `filter`, `flat`, `toSorted`, `toSpliced`.

sections.heading: Searching & Iteration Utilities
sections.content: Array lookup methods simplify element retrieval and condition testing across elements.
bulletPoints: `indexOf()` / `includes()`: Value equality search.
`find()` / `findIndex()`: Predicate condition callback search.
`some()` / `every()`: Boolean validation across array elements.

keyTakeaways: Distinguish mutating vs non-mutating array operations.
Use `includes`/`find` for searching arrays efficiently.
React state updates require non-mutating array copies.

codeExamples.title: Slice vs Splice Demonstration
codeExamples.description: Non-mutating slice vs mutating splice array operations.

mcqs.question: Which method mutates original array in place?
mcqs.explanation: `splice()` modifies original array in place by deleting/inserting items.

mcqs.question: What does `array.find(fn)` return if no element matches predicate function?
mcqs.explanation: `find()` returns first matching element, or `undefined` if no match is found.

mcqs.question: Which array method returns true if AT LEAST ONE element matches condition?
mcqs.explanation: `some()` returns true as soon as one element satisfies predicate function.

mcqs.question: What is logged by `[1, 2, 3].concat([4, 5])`?
mcqs.explanation: `concat()` joins arrays into a new shallow-copied array without mutating inputs.

mcqs.question: What is default sorting behavior of `[10, 2, 5].sort()` without comparator callback?
mcqs.explanation: Default `sort()` converts elements to strings, sorting alphabetically (`'10'` comes before `'2'`).

title: Destructuring
summary: Unpacking values from arrays and properties from objects into distinct variables with defaults and renaming.

explanation.overview: Destructuring assignment syntax enables unpacking values from arrays or properties from objects into distinct variables concisely.

sections.heading: Object Destructuring
sections.content: Extracts properties by matching key names. Supports default values, variable renaming, and nested extraction.
bulletPoints: Renaming: `{ oldKey: newVarName }`.
Default Values: `{ key = 'defaultVal' }` triggered only when property is `undefined`.
Nested Extraction: `{ user: { name } }`.

sections.heading: Array Destructuring
sections.content: Extracts elements by positional index. Supports skipping items and rest patterns.
bulletPoints: Positional Matching: `const [first, second] = arr`.
Skipping Items: `const [a, , c] = arr`.
Swapping Variables: `[a, b] = [b, a]`.

keyTakeaways: Object destructuring matches keys; array destructuring matches position.
Default values trigger only when extracted value is `undefined` (not `null`).
Easily swap variables using `[a, b] = [b, a]`.

codeExamples.title: Object & Array Destructuring
codeExamples.description: Renaming, defaults, nested extraction, and array swapping.

mcqs.question: What is value of `b` in `const { a, b = 10 } = { a: 5, b: null }`?
mcqs.explanation: Default values trigger ONLY when value is `undefined`. Since `b` is `null`, `null` is preserved.

mcqs.question: How do you rename property `name` to `userName` during object destructuring?
mcqs.explanation: The colon syntax `{ property: newVariableName }` renames destructured variable.

mcqs.question: What is logged by `const [, y] = [10, 20, 30]`?
mcqs.explanation: Leading empty comma skips index 0, assigning index 1 (`20`) to variable `y`.

mcqs.question: What occurs when attempting to destructure `null` `const { x } = null`?
mcqs.explanation: Destructuring `null` or `undefined` throws TypeError because they cannot be converted to objects.

mcqs.question: How do you capture remaining array elements into variable `rest` during array destructuring?
mcqs.explanation: Rest element `...rest` captures all remaining uncollected array elements and must be placed last.

title: Spread/rest
summary: Spread operator `...` for expanding iterables/objects vs Rest operator `...` for gathering parameters.

explanation.overview: The `...` syntax serves dual purposes in JS: **Spread** expands elements of iterable/object into elements, while **Rest** collects multiple elements into single array parameter.

sections.heading: Spread Operator (Expansion)
sections.content: Used in function calls, array literals, and object literals to shallow copy or merge data structures.
bulletPoints: Array Merge: `[...arr1, ...arr2]`.
Object Shallow Merge: `{ ...defaults, ...userOptions }`.
Function Call Arguments: `Math.max(...numArray)`.

sections.heading: Rest Operator (Collection)
sections.content: Used in function parameter signatures and destructuring assignments to collect residual items into array.
bulletPoints: Function Rest Parameter: `function fn(first, ...others)`.
Destructuring Rest: `const { id, ...data } = userObj`.
Rule: Rest parameter must be last item in signature.

keyTakeaways: Spread expands iterables; Rest gathers elements into array.
Spread creates shallow copies of objects/arrays.
Rest parameters replace legacy `arguments` object in ES6 functions.

codeExamples.title: Spread vs Rest Operators
codeExamples.description: Rest parameter in function vs Spread operator merging objects.

mcqs.question: What is the restriction on rest parameters in function definitions?
options: Can only collect up to 5 arguments
Must be the final parameter in parameter list
Cannot be used in arrow functions
mcqs.explanation: A rest parameter `...args` must always be the last parameter in function signature.

mcqs.question: What is logged by `const a = [1, 2]; const b = [...a, 3]; console.log(b)`?
mcqs.explanation: Spread `...a` unpacks elements `1, 2` directly into outer array, giving `[1, 2, 3]`.

mcqs.question: What type of object does rest parameter `...args` produce inside a function?
options: Array instance with full array methods
mcqs.explanation: Rest parameters produce genuine JavaScript `Array` instances with map/filter/reduce access.

mcqs.question: What happens when keys collide in object spread `{ ...{ a: 1 }, ...{ a: 2 } }`?
options: a is 2 (later keys overwrite earlier keys)
mcqs.explanation: When spreading objects with duplicate keys, later spread properties overwrite earlier ones.

mcqs.question: How do you pass array elements as separate arguments to `Math.max()`?
mcqs.explanation: `Math.max(...arr)` spreads array elements as individual numerical positional arguments.

title: map/filter/reduce
summary: Functional array transformations: map (1-to-1 transform), filter (subset selection), reduce (accumulator aggregation).

explanation.overview: `map`, `filter`, and `reduce` form core foundation of functional array processing in JS, creating new output without mutating source arrays.

sections.heading: map & filter
sections.content: `map()` transforms every element 1-to-1, returning array of same length. `filter()` returns subset containing elements that return truthy for predicate function.
bulletPoints: `map(fn)`: Same length, transformed elements.
`filter(fn)`: Equal or smaller length, matching elements.
Chaining: `arr.filter(...).map(...)` combines transformations.

sections.heading: reduce Mechanics
sections.content: `reduce((acc, curr) => ..., initialValue)` iterates array passing single accumulator value along steps to condense array into single value (number, object, array).
bulletPoints: Always pass `initialValue` to avoid error on empty arrays.
Can replace both map and filter in single pass.
Ideal for grouping data, summing totals, and pipe operations.

keyTakeaways: `map` transforms 1-to-1, `filter` subsets, `reduce` aggregates.
All three methods return new results without mutating original array.
Always provide initial accumulator value to `reduce`.

codeExamples.title: Map, Filter, Reduce Pipeline
codeExamples.description: Filtering even numbers, doubling them, and calculating total sum.

mcqs.question: What is output length of `[1, 2, 3].map(x => x > 1)`?
mcqs.explanation: `map()` always returns array of identical length to original input array.

mcqs.question: What happens if `reduce()` is called on an empty array without initialValue?
mcqs.explanation: Calling `reduce()` on an empty array without supplying initial value throws TypeError.

mcqs.question: Which method would you use to group an array of user objects by role into a map object?
mcqs.explanation: `reduce()` aggregates elements into complex accumulated shapes like grouping objects.

mcqs.question: What does `[1, 2, 3, 4].filter(x => false)` return?
mcqs.explanation: If predicate returns false for all elements, `filter()` returns a new empty array.

mcqs.question: What is logged by `[10, 20].reduce((acc, curr) => acc + curr)` with no initial value specified?
mcqs.explanation: Without initial value on non-empty array, first element (`10`) becomes initial accumulator.

title: Hoisting
summary: Hoisting mechanics of function declarations, var variables, and let/const TDZ behavior.

explanation.overview: Hoisting is JS execution context creation phase where declarations are allocated in memory before code execution starts.

sections.heading: Functions vs Variables
sections.content: Function declarations (`function foo(){}`) hoist with their complete implementation body. `var` variables hoist initialized as `undefined`. `let` and `const` hoist into TDZ without initialization.
bulletPoints: Function declarations can be invoked before definition line.
Calling a `var` function expression before declaration throws `TypeError: foo is not a function`.
Accessing `let` or `const` before declaration throws `ReferenceError`.

sections.heading: Declaration Precedence
sections.content: Function declarations take precedence over `var` variable declarations when identifiers collide.
bulletPoints: Functions hoist above var declarations.
Subsequent var assignments overwrite function identifiers at execution time.

keyTakeaways: Function declarations hoist completely.
Var declarations hoist initialized with undefined.
Let and const hoist into TDZ.

codeExamples.title: Hoisting Behavior
codeExamples.description: Demonstrating function declaration hoisting vs function expression.

mcqs.question: What is output by `foo(); function foo() { console.log('bar'); }`?
mcqs.explanation: Function declarations are fully hoisted and callable anywhere in scope.

mcqs.question: What happens when invoking `baz()` before `var baz = () => {};`?
options: Throws TypeError: baz is not a function
mcqs.explanation: `var baz` hoists as `undefined`, and `undefined()` throws a TypeError.

mcqs.question: Which declaration type has highest priority during creation phase hoisting?
mcqs.explanation: Function declarations are hoisted before variable declarations.

mcqs.question: Are ES6 Class declarations hoisted in JavaScript?
mcqs.explanation: Classes hoist into Temporal Dead Zone; accessing them early throws ReferenceError.

mcqs.question: What is printed by `var a = 1; function test() { a = 2; return; function a() {} } test(); console.log(a);`?
mcqs.explanation: Inner `function a() {}` hoists inside `test()`, creating a local identifier `a`, leaving global `a` unchanged at 1.

title: Closures
summary: Lexical environment retention, private variables, and memory behavior in JS closures.

explanation.overview: A closure is a function bundled together with references to its outer lexical environment. Inner functions retain access to outer variables even after outer function execution context finishes.

sections.heading: Closure Mechanics
sections.content: Functions preserve internal `[[Environment]]` pointers. When an inner function outlives outer execution, outer environment variables persist in heap memory.
bulletPoints: Data Encapsulation: Creates private variables unreachable from outer scope.
State Preservation: Used in currying, memoization, and event handlers.
Memory Lifecycle: Variables remain in memory until closure references are cleaned.

sections.heading: Common Use Cases
sections.content: Closures power factory functions, state management, and private modules.
bulletPoints: Encapsulating state in custom hooks and utilities.
Preserving loop counter variables in async callbacks.

keyTakeaways: Closures remember their lexical environment.
Enable private variables and state encapsulation.
Be mindful of memory leaks from uncleaned closure references.

codeExamples.title: Private Counter Closure
codeExamples.description: Encapsulating count variable using closure functions.

mcqs.question: What defines a JavaScript closure?
options: A function bundled with access to its outer lexical scope
A function that takes no parameters
mcqs.explanation: A closure allows an inner function to access variables from its enclosing lexical scope.

mcqs.question: What is logged by `for (var i=0; i<3; i++) { setTimeout(()=>console.log(i),10); }`?
mcqs.explanation: `var i` is function-scoped; all callbacks close over the same mutated `i` variable which equals 3 after loop completes.

mcqs.question: How do you fix the classic var loop timer closure issue using modern JS?
mcqs.explanation: `let` creates a distinct block binding for `i` in each loop iteration.

mcqs.question: Which design pattern relies heavily on closures for encapsulation?
mcqs.explanation: The Module Pattern uses closures to expose public APIs while keeping inner state private.

mcqs.question: When can variables captured by a closure be garbage collected?
options: When all references to inner closure function are removed
mcqs.explanation: Garbage collector cannot free captured closure variables while an active reference to the inner function exists.

title: this
summary: Dynamic binding of `this`: Implicit binding, explicit binding, new binding, and arrow function lexical this.

explanation.overview: In JavaScript, `this` is evaluated dynamically based on how a function is called, except for arrow functions which bind `this` lexically.

sections.heading: Binding Rules Priority
sections.content:
1. `new` keyword binding (creates new instance).
2. Explicit binding (`call`, `apply`, `bind`).
3. Implicit binding (object method call `obj.fn()`).
4. Default binding (global window / undefined in strict mode).
bulletPoints: `new` creates new object bound to `this`.
Implicit: `obj.method()` sets `this` to `obj`.
Strict mode: standalone function call sets `this` to `undefined`.

sections.heading: Arrow Functions & lexical this
sections.content: Arrow functions do not have their own `this`. They inherit `this` from enclosing lexical execution context at creation time.
bulletPoints: Cannot be re-bound with `call`/`apply`/`bind`.
Ideal for event listeners and timer callbacks inside class/object methods.

keyTakeaways: Regular function `this` depends on invocation site.
Arrow functions capture `this` lexically.
`new` binding takes highest priority.

codeExamples.title: Implicit vs Arrow Function this
codeExamples.description: Comparing standard function invocation vs arrow function.

mcqs.question: What is `this` inside a non-strict mode regular function called standalone `foo()`?
mcqs.explanation: In non-strict mode, standalone calls default `this` to global object.

mcqs.question: What is `this` inside a standalone regular function call in `'use strict'` mode?
mcqs.explanation: Strict mode prevents default global coercion, setting `this` to `undefined`.

mcqs.question: How does an arrow function determine its `this` value?
mcqs.explanation: Arrow functions capture `this` from their outer lexical scope when created.

mcqs.question: Which binding rule has the highest precedence?
mcqs.explanation: `new` keyword binding overrides explicit and implicit bindings.

mcqs.question: What happens when using `.bind(obj)` on an arrow function?
mcqs.explanation: Arrow function `this` is permanently locked lexically and cannot be changed by `.bind()`.

title: call/apply/bind
summary: Explicitly setting function execution context: call (arg list), apply (arg array), bind (returns bound function).

explanation.overview: `call`, `apply`, and `bind` are `Function.prototype` methods used to explicitly control the `this` context during function invocation.

sections.heading: call vs apply
sections.content: Both execute the function immediately with explicit `this`. `call()` accepts individual comma-separated arguments, while `apply()` accepts an array of arguments.
bulletPoints: `fn.call(ctx, arg1, arg2)`: Immediate execution with argument list.
`fn.apply(ctx, [arg1, arg2])`: Immediate execution with argument array.
Use cases: Method borrowing (`Array.prototype.slice.call(arguments)`).

sections.heading: bind Method
sections.content: `bind()` creates and returns a new function with `this` locked to specified target object, supporting partial application (currying).
bulletPoints: Does not execute function immediately.
Returns bound function copy.
Allows pre-setting initial function arguments.

keyTakeaways: `call` takes comma list, `apply` takes array.
`bind` returns new permanently bound function.
Useful for method borrowing and maintaining context in callbacks.

codeExamples.title: Explicit Binding Example
codeExamples.description: Borrowing method using call, apply, and bind.

mcqs.question: What is the primary difference between `call` and `apply`?
options: call takes array of args, apply takes list
call takes comma-separated args, apply takes array of args
bind is synchronous, call is async
mcqs.explanation: `call` passes arguments individually; `apply` passes arguments as an array.

mcqs.question: What does `func.bind(ctx)` return?
options: A new function bound to ctx
mcqs.explanation: `bind()` returns a new wrapper function with bound `this` context.

mcqs.question: What happens if null or undefined is passed as first argument to `call` in non-strict mode?
mcqs.explanation: In non-strict mode, `null` or `undefined` passed as `this` context defaults to global object (`window`/`global`).

mcqs.question: What is partial application in `bind`?
options: Pre-filling initial arguments when calling bind
Binding only certain properties of object
mcqs.explanation: Passing initial arguments to `bind(ctx, arg1)` pre-fills those arguments for future invocations.

mcqs.question: Can a function bound with `const f = fn.bind(obj1)` be re-bound using `f.bind(obj2)`?
options: No, initial bind context cannot be overridden
mcqs.explanation: A bound function returned by `.bind()` cannot have its `this` rebound by subsequent `.bind()` calls.

title: Prototypes
summary: Prototypal inheritance model, `prototype` vs `__proto__`, prototype chain lookup mechanism.

explanation.overview: JavaScript utilizes prototypal inheritance. Objects have an internal link `[[Prototype]]` pointing to another object. Property lookup traverses up this prototype chain until found or reaching `null`.

sections.heading: Prototype Chain Lookup
sections.content: When accessing `obj.prop`, JS first checks `obj` own properties. If not found, it checks `obj.__proto__`, following the chain up to `Object.prototype`, and finally `null`.
bulletPoints: `prototype`: Property on constructor functions used to build `[[Prototype]]` link for instance objects.
`__proto__`: Getter/setter accessor for instance object's internal `[[Prototype]]` link.
`Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)`: Standard method to access an object's prototype.

sections.heading: Object.create & Inheritance
sections.content: `Object.create(proto)` creates a new object with specified prototype object, enabling direct inheritance without constructor functions.
bulletPoints: Memory Optimization: Shared methods reside on prototype rather than duplicated per instance.
`hasOwnProperty()`: Checks if property exists directly on instance vs inherited.

keyTakeaways: JS inheritance relies on prototype delegation chain.
Shared methods belong on `Constructor.prototype` to save memory.
`Object.prototype` is top of normal chain, referencing `null`.

codeExamples.title: Prototypal Inheritance
codeExamples.description: Creating inheritance chain with Object.create and constructor prototypes.

mcqs.question: What is at the top end of standard JavaScript prototype chain?
mcqs.explanation: `Object.prototype.__proto__` is `null`, terminating property lookups.

mcqs.question: What method checks if a property exists directly on an object rather than inherited from prototype?
mcqs.explanation: `obj.hasOwnProperty('prop')` returns true only for direct non-inherited instance properties.

mcqs.question: What is `__proto__` of instance created via `const p = new Person()`?
mcqs.explanation: Instance `p.__proto__` links directly to constructor's `Person.prototype` object.

mcqs.question: What does `Object.create(null)` produce?
options: An empty object with no prototype chain
mcqs.explanation: `Object.create(null)` creates a dictionary object without any prototype properties or methods like `toString`.

mcqs.question: Why are methods placed on `Constructor.prototype` instead of inside constructor function body?
options: To share single method instance across all objects saving memory
mcqs.explanation: Putting methods on `.prototype` avoids creating separate copies of function in memory for every instance.

title: Classes
summary: ES6 class syntax syntactic sugar, constructors, extends inheritance, super(), and private fields.

explanation.overview: ES6 classes provide cleaner syntactic sugar over prototype-based inheritance. Classes support constructors, instance methods, static methods, getters/setters, and private fields (`#field`).

sections.heading: Class Structure & Inheritance
sections.content: `class` defines object template. `extends` sets up prototypal inheritance, and derived class constructors must invoke `super()` before accessing `this`.
bulletPoints: `constructor()`: Special method for initializing new object instances.
`super()`: Calls parent class constructor.
`static`: Methods/properties attached directly to Class constructor, not instances.

sections.heading: Private Fields & Strict Mode
sections.content: Class bodies execute in strict mode automatically. ES2022 private fields (`#privateVar`) provide true hard privacy enforced at runtime.
bulletPoints: `#field`: Truly private field inaccessible outside class body.
Class declarations are not hoisted into initialized state (reside in TDZ).

keyTakeaways: Classes are built on prototype delegation under the hood.
Derived classes require `super()` before using `this`.
Use `#field` syntax for private state encapsulation.

codeExamples.title: ES6 Class Inheritance & Private Fields
codeExamples.description: Parent class, extends, super, static method, and private fields.

mcqs.question: What must be called in a derived class constructor before referencing `this`?
mcqs.explanation: Derived class constructors must call `super()` first to initialize parent class instance binding.

mcqs.question: How are private class fields declared in modern ES2022 JavaScript?
mcqs.explanation: Prefixing field names with `#` creates a private field enforced natively by JS engine.

mcqs.question: How are static methods called on a class `class Utility { static run() {} }`?
mcqs.explanation: Static methods are invoked on Class constructor itself (`Utility.run()`), not on instances.

mcqs.question: What mode do class bodies execute in automatically?
mcqs.explanation: All code inside ES6 class bodies runs in strict mode automatically.

mcqs.question: Are class declarations hoisted like standard `function` declarations?
options: No, they reside in TDZ like let/const
mcqs.explanation: Class declarations are hoisted but remain uninitialized in TDZ; invoking them early throws ReferenceError.

title: Modules
summary: ES6 Modules (import/export), CommonJS (require/module.exports), tree-shaking, static analysis.

explanation.overview: JavaScript supports two primary module systems: ES6 Modules (ESM) standard (`import`/`export`) and CommonJS (CJS) legacy Node system (`require`/`module.exports`).

sections.heading: ES6 Modules (ESM)
sections.content: ESM modules are statically analyzed at compile time, enabling bundlers to perform dead code elimination (tree-shaking). ESM exports live read-only bindings.
bulletPoints: Named Exports: `export const foo = 1; import { foo } from './file.js';`.
Default Export: `export default App; import App from './App.js';`.
Strict Mode: ESM files implicitly run in strict mode.

sections.heading: CommonJS (CJS) vs ESM
sections.content: CommonJS is synchronous and dynamic (`require()` can be called conditionally inside functions). ESM imports must reside at top level of module.
bulletPoints: CommonJS: Dynamic runtime loading (`require()`).
ESM: Static top-level analysis (`import`), dynamic import via `import()` promise function.
Bindings: CJS exports value copies; ESM exports live variable bindings.

keyTakeaways: ESM uses static `import`/`export`; CommonJS uses `require`/`module.exports`.
ESM static nature enables tree-shaking dead code elimination.
ESM exports live bindings; CJS exports value copies.

codeExamples.title: ESM Named & Default Exports
codeExamples.description: Exporting named utilities and default class component.

mcqs.question: What is primary advantage of ES6 Modules (ESM) static syntax over CommonJS?
options: Enables static analysis and bundler tree-shaking
mcqs.explanation: Static `import`/`export` statements allow build tools to analyze dependency trees and prune dead code (tree-shaking).

mcqs.question: How do live bindings in ESM differ from CommonJS exports?
options: ESM exported variables update automatically in importer when changed in exporter
mcqs.explanation: ESM exports live read-only variable bindings; if source module changes exported variable, importers see updated value.

mcqs.question: How do you perform dynamic conditional module loading in ESM?
options: Using dynamic import() which returns a Promise
mcqs.explanation: Dynamic `import('./module.js')` function can be invoked anywhere conditionally and returns a Promise resolving to module.

mcqs.question: What mode do ES6 modules execute in by default?
mcqs.explanation: ES6 modules are implicitly strict mode; `'use strict'` declaration is not required.

mcqs.question: How many default exports can a single ES6 module file contain?
mcqs.explanation: A module can have multiple named exports, but at most ONE `export default`.

title: Error handling
summary: try/catch/finally blocks, Custom Error classes, unhandled promise rejections, window.onerror.

explanation.overview: Robust error handling prevents unhandled exceptions from crashing applications. JS provides `try...catch...finally` statements and custom Error classes.

sections.heading: try...catch...finally Mechanics
sections.content: `try` wraps code that may throw exceptions. `catch(err)` catches threw errors. `finally` executes unconditionally for cleanup.
bulletPoints: `throw`: Raises built-in `Error` instance or custom error.
`finally`: Executes even if `return` statement exists inside `try` or `catch`.
Catch Binding: ES2019 allows optional catch binding `catch {}`.

sections.heading: Async Errors & Global Handlers
sections.content: Synchronous `try/catch` cannot catch async errors thrown inside callbacks or promises unless `await` is used. Use global listeners for uncaught errors.
bulletPoints: Browser: `window.addEventListener('unhandledrejection')` and `window.onerror`.
Node.js: `process.on('uncaughtException')` and `process.on('unhandledRejection')`.
Custom Errors: Extend built-in `Error` class (`class AppError extends Error`).

keyTakeaways: Use `try...catch` for synchronous code and `await` calls.
Extend `Error` class to create domain-specific custom exceptions.
Register global unhandled rejection handlers to log uncaught async errors.

codeExamples.title: Custom Error Class & Handling
codeExamples.description: Extending Error class with statusCode and custom try/catch.

mcqs.question: What happens if code inside `try` block returns value `return 10`, but `finally` block contains `return 20`?
mcqs.explanation: A `return` statement inside `finally` block overrides any previous `return` statements from `try` or `catch` blocks.

mcqs.question: Can standard synchronous `try { setTimeout(() => { throw new Error('boom'); }, 100); } catch(e) {}` catch the error?
options: No, because callback executes asynchronously after try block exits
mcqs.explanation: Synchronous `try/catch` exits immediately; async callback executes later on event loop, escaping catch block.

mcqs.question: How do you create a custom error class in modern ES6 JavaScript?
mcqs.explanation: Custom errors extend native built-in `Error` class and invoke `super(message)` inside constructor.

mcqs.question: Which window event fires when a Promise rejects without any `.catch()` handler attached?
mcqs.explanation: Browsers dispatch `unhandledrejection` event when a promise is rejected without rejection handler.

mcqs.question: What is ES2019 optional catch binding feature?
options: Omitting error parameter in `catch {}` when error variable is unused
Catching multiple error types in one line
mcqs.explanation: Optional catch binding allows writing `catch {}` without specifying unused `catch (err)` parameter.

title: Promises
summary: Asynchronous operations, Promise states (Pending, Fulfilled, Rejected), then/catch/finally chaining.

explanation.overview: A Promise represents eventual completion (or failure) of an asynchronous operation and its resulting value, preventing callback hell.

sections.heading: Promise States & Lifecycle
sections.content: A Promise is always in one of 3 mutually exclusive states: **Pending** (initial), **Fulfilled** (resolved successfully), or **Rejected** (failed with error). Once settled, state transitions are immutable.
bulletPoints: Pending -> Fulfilled (`resolve(val)`).
Pending -> Rejected (`reject(err)`).
Settled: State cannot change after settling.

sections.heading: Chaining & Error Propagation
sections.content: Methods `.then()`, `.catch()`, and `.finally()` return new promises, allowing asynchronous method chaining.
bulletPoints: `.then(onFulfilled)`: Handles fulfillment value, returns new Promise.
`.catch(onRejected)`: Catches errors thrown anywhere upstream in chain.
`.finally(onSettled)`: Executes cleanup code regardless of success or failure.

keyTakeaways: Promises have 3 states: Pending, Fulfilled, Rejected.
Promises are settled immutably.
Always include `.catch()` or handle rejections to prevent unhandled rejection crashes.

codeExamples.title: Creating & Chaining Promises
codeExamples.description: Constructing Promise instance and chaining then/catch/finally handlers.

mcqs.question: What are 3 possible states of a JavaScript Promise?
mcqs.explanation: A Promise exists in Pending state until transition to settled state: Fulfilled or Rejected.

mcqs.question: What does calling `.then()` on a Promise return?
mcqs.explanation: `.then()` always returns a new Promise, allowing chaining.

mcqs.question: What happens if an exception is thrown inside a `.then()` callback?
options: The returned Promise transitions to Rejected state
mcqs.explanation: Any error thrown inside `.then()` handler automatically rejects returned downstream Promise.

mcqs.question: When does `.finally()` callback execute?
options: Regardless of whether promise fulfills or rejects
mcqs.explanation: `.finally()` runs whenever promise settles, whether fulfilled or rejected.

mcqs.question: Can a settled (fulfilled or rejected) Promise change state again?
options: Yes, calling resolve again updates value
No, state transitions are immutable once settled
mcqs.explanation: Promises are permanently locked once settled; subsequent resolve/reject calls are ignored.

title: async/await
summary: Syntactic sugar over promises, sequential vs parallel async execution, try/catch error handling.

explanation.overview: `async` and `await` keywords make asynchronous Promise code read synchronously, improving clarity while maintaining non-blocking performance.

sections.heading: async Functions & await Operator
sections.content: Declaring a function `async` forces it to return a Promise. `await` pauses execution of async function until Promise resolves/rejects.
bulletPoints: `async`: Wraps return value in resolved Promise.
`await`: Unwraps resolved value of Promise (can only be used inside async function or top-level ESM).
Error handling: Wrapped inside standard `try...catch` blocks.

sections.heading: Sequential vs Parallel Pitfall
sections.content: Awaiting promises sequentially when independence exists creates performance bottlenecks (`waterfall effect`). Trigger tasks concurrently using `Promise.all()`.
bulletPoints: Sequential: `await fn1(); await fn2();` (Total time = t1 + t2).
Parallel: `await Promise.all([fn1(), fn2()])` (Total time = max(t1, t2)).

keyTakeaways: `async` functions always return a Promise.
`await` pauses async function execution until Promise settles.
Avoid sequential awaits for independent operations; execute concurrently.

codeExamples.title: Async/Await with Error Handling
codeExamples.description: Fetching data asynchronously using try/catch.

mcqs.question: What does an `async` function return if it explicitly returns string `'hello'`?
mcqs.explanation: `async` functions always wrap returned values in a resolved Promise.

mcqs.question: What happens when `await` encounters a rejected Promise inside try/catch?
options: Throws the rejection reason as a catchable error
mcqs.explanation: `await` unwraps promise rejections by throwing them as exceptions catchable in `try...catch` blocks.

mcqs.question: What is performance risk of writing `const a = await getA(); const b = await getB();` when A and B are independent?
options: Waterfall latency where total execution time equals sum of both requests
mcqs.explanation: Sequential awaiting forces `getB()` to wait until `getA()` resolves, doubling total latency needlessly.

mcqs.question: Where can `await` operator be used in modern JavaScript?
options: Only inside functions declared with `async` or at top level of ES modules
mcqs.explanation: `await` is only valid inside `async` functions or top-level ES Module scope.

mcqs.question: Does `await` block the main browser UI execution thread?
options: No, it yields control back to event loop while waiting for Promise settlement
mcqs.explanation: `await` non-blocking pause yields execution thread to event loop, allowing UI and other tasks to run.

title: Promise.all/allSettled/race/any
summary: Concurrency helpers: Promise.all (all resolve or fail-fast), allSettled (wait for all), race (first settled), any (first fulfilled).

explanation.overview: JavaScript provides 4 static Promise combinator methods to manage concurrent asynchronous operations with distinct failure and completion strategies.

sections.heading: Promise.all vs Promise.allSettled
sections.content: `Promise.all` waits for all promises to resolve, but fails fast on first rejection. `Promise.allSettled` waits for all promises to settle regardless of outcome.
bulletPoints: `Promise.all([p1, p2])`: Fulfills with array of values if ALL resolve; rejects immediately if ANY rejects.
`Promise.allSettled([p1, p2])`: Resolves when ALL settle with array of `{status, value|reason}` objects.

sections.heading: Promise.race vs Promise.any
sections.content: `Promise.race` settles as soon as FIRST promise settles (resolve or reject). `Promise.any` settles as soon as FIRST promise fulfills, ignoring rejections unless ALL reject (AggregateError).
bulletPoints: `Promise.race([p1, p2])`: First to finish wins (resolve or reject). Useful for timeouts.
`Promise.any([p1, p2])`: First fulfilled wins. Throws AggregateError if all reject.

keyTakeaways: `Promise.all` fails fast on first rejection.
`Promise.allSettled` guarantees waiting for all promises to finish.
`Promise.race` settles on first result; `Promise.any` settles on first success.

codeExamples.title: Promise Combinators Comparison
codeExamples.description: Demonstrating Promise.all vs Promise.allSettled.

mcqs.question: What happens in `Promise.all([p1, p2, p3])` if `p2` rejects after 10ms while `p1` and `p3` resolve at 100ms?
options: Returns values of p1 and p3
mcqs.explanation: `Promise.all` fails fast and rejects as soon as any single promise in array rejects.

mcqs.question: Which combinator guarantees that it will NEVER reject as long as an array of promises is passed?
mcqs.explanation: `Promise.allSettled` always fulfills with an array describing outcome status for every promise.

mcqs.question: What error is thrown by `Promise.any()` when ALL promises in array reject?
mcqs.explanation: If all promises passed to `Promise.any()` reject, it rejects with an `AggregateError` containing array of rejection reasons.

mcqs.question: Which combinator is ideal for setting request timeouts (e.g. race API request against a timeout promise)?
mcqs.explanation: `Promise.race` completes as soon as first promise settles (whether API response resolves or timeout promise rejects).

mcqs.question: What is returned by `Promise.all([])` when passed an empty array?
mcqs.explanation: Passing an empty array to `Promise.all([])` returns a promise fulfilled with empty array `[]` synchronously.

title: Event loop
summary: Single-threaded runtime, Call Stack, Task Queue (Macrotasks), Microtask Queue execution priority.

explanation.overview: JavaScript executes code in a single-threaded runtime loop. The Event Loop monitors Call Stack and processes Microtasks and Macrotasks when stack becomes empty.

sections.heading: Call Stack & Concurrency
sections.content: JS call stack executes frame functions synchronously (LIFO). Long-running synchronous functions block stack execution, rendering browser UI frozen.
bulletPoints: Call Stack: Executes synchronous code frames.
Web APIs: Browser offloads async tasks (timers, fetch) to background threads.

sections.heading: Execution Priority Loop
sections.content:
1. Execute synchronous call stack code until empty.
2. Drain entire Microtask queue completely.
3. Render UI updates (if needed).
4. Pick ONE Macrotask from task queue and push to stack.
5. Repeat.
bulletPoints: Microtask Queue drained completely before next macrotask.
Single-threaded non-blocking I/O model.

keyTakeaways: JS single-threaded event loop processes tasks asynchronously.
Microtasks drain completely before next Macrotask executes.
Avoid blocking call stack with long synchronous CPU computation.

codeExamples.title: Event Loop Execution Order
codeExamples.description: Predicting execution output across call stack, microtasks, and macrotasks.

mcqs.question: What is primary role of the JavaScript Event Loop?
options: To compile JavaScript to machine bytecode
To monitor Call Stack and push queued async callbacks when stack is empty
mcqs.explanation: The Event Loop continuously checks call stack; when empty, it pushes queued microtasks and macrotasks to stack.

mcqs.question: What happens if synchronous function loop `while(true){}` runs on main JS thread?
options: Event loop blocks; UI freezes and async callbacks cannot execute
Event loop skips while loop after 1 second
mcqs.explanation: Synchronous loops lock call stack, preventing Event Loop from processing any queued events or rendering UI updates.

mcqs.question: Which queue has higher execution priority when call stack clears?
mcqs.explanation: Microtasks always execute before the next macrotask can be pulled from task queue.

mcqs.question: How many macrotasks does Event Loop process per iteration before re-checking microtasks?
mcqs.explanation: Event Loop processes exactly ONE macrotask, then immediately drains microtask queue completely.

mcqs.question: Where are browser `fetch()` API network operations processed?
options: Offloaded to Browser Web APIs background threads
mcqs.explanation: Browser Web APIs handle network operations in background C++ threads, pushing callback/promise handlers to JS queues upon completion.

title: Microtasks/macrotasks
summary: Task Queue differentiation: Microtasks (Promises, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver) vs Macrotasks (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, setImmediate).

explanation.overview: Asynchronous tasks in JS are divided into Microtasks and Macrotasks. Microtasks run immediately after stack clears, draining completely before Macrotasks.

sections.heading: Microtask Queue
sections.content: Microtasks include Promise `.then()/.catch()/.finally()`, `queueMicrotask()`, `process.nextTick` (Node.js), and `MutationObserver`.
bulletPoints: Executed immediately after call stack empties.
Queue drained to 0 items before browser layout/paint or next macrotask.
Infinite microtask recursion starves UI rendering and macrotasks.

sections.heading: Macrotask (Task) Queue
sections.content: Macrotasks include `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `setImmediate` (Node), I/O operations, and UI user interactions.
bulletPoints: Executed one by one after microtask queue is fully drained.
Browser can perform DOM rendering between macrotasks.

keyTakeaways: Microtasks (Promises) run before Macrotasks (setTimeout).
Microtask queue drains completely before next Macrotask runs.
Recursive microtasks starve rendering and freeze app UI.

codeExamples.title: Microtask vs Macrotask Execution Order
codeExamples.description: Demonstrating promise microtasks running before timer macrotasks.

mcqs.question: Which operation creates a Microtask?
mcqs.explanation: Promise handlers `.then()` register callbacks into the Microtask Queue.

mcqs.question: What happens if a microtask schedules another microtask recursively without stopping?
options: Microtask queue drains endlessly, starving Macrotasks and freezing UI rendering
Event loop automatically switches to Macrotask queue
mcqs.explanation: Because the microtask queue must drain completely to 0, recursive microtasks starve macrotasks and freeze browser UI.

mcqs.question: Which API allows manually enqueueing a microtask without creating a Promise?
mcqs.explanation: `queueMicrotask(fn)` enqueues callback directly into JS microtask queue.

mcqs.question: In Node.js event loop, which queue executes even before standard Promise microtasks?
mcqs.explanation: In Node.js, `process.nextTick` queue runs prior to standard Promise microtask queue at tick transitions.

mcqs.question: Is DOM rendering performed before or after microtask queue draining?
options: After microtask queue is completely drained
mcqs.explanation: Browser UI rendering occurs AFTER microtask queue is fully emptied, prior to running next macrotask.

title: Memory
summary: JavaScript memory model: Call Stack (primitive values, frame pointers) vs Heap (reference objects).

explanation.overview: JavaScript manages memory automatically. Primitives and execution frames are stored on Call Stack, while reference objects reside in Heap memory.

sections.heading: Stack vs Heap Allocation
sections.content: The **Stack** stores fixed-size static primitive values (numbers, booleans, symbols, null, undefined) and function frame pointers. The **Heap** allocates dynamic unbounded memory for Objects, Arrays, and Functions.
bulletPoints: Stack Memory: Fast, fixed size, LIFO function execution context stack.
Heap Memory: Unstructured large memory pool for reference objects.
Variable References: Stack stores heap memory addresses for objects.

sections.heading: Value vs Reference Assignment
sections.content: Primitives are copied by value. Objects are copied by reference address pointer.
bulletPoints: Primitive Copy: Independent value duplication.
Reference Copy: Mutating object via new variable alters original object in heap.

keyTakeaways: Primitives stored on Stack; Objects stored in Heap.
Primitives copied by value; Objects copied by reference address pointer.
Unreachable heap objects are eligible for Garbage Collection.

codeExamples.title: Stack Value vs Heap Reference
codeExamples.description: Demonstrating primitive copy by value vs object copy by reference pointer.

mcqs.question: Where are JavaScript primitive values (e.g. booleans, small numbers) stored in memory?
mcqs.explanation: Primitives of fixed size are allocated on Call Stack within execution context frames.

mcqs.question: What happens when variable `b` is assigned an existing object variable `a` (`b = a`)?
options: Creates deep clone of object in heap
b receives reference address pointer pointing to same heap memory location
mcqs.explanation: Object assignments copy memory reference pointer, so both variables point to identical heap object.

mcqs.question: Where are complex objects, arrays, and functions stored in memory?
mcqs.explanation: Dynamic variable-sized complex types reside in unstructured Heap memory.

mcqs.question: What is logged by `const x = { n: 1 }; const y = { n: 1 }; console.log(x === y);`?
mcqs.explanation: `===` compares reference memory addresses for objects; `x` and `y` reference distinct heap allocations.

mcqs.question: How are variable bindings managed on Call Stack during function call and return?
options: Push execution frame onto stack on call, pop and reclaim frame memory upon return
mcqs.explanation: Function invocation pushes frame onto call stack; returning pops frame and reclaims stack space.

title: Garbage collection
summary: Automatic memory management, Mark-and-Sweep algorithm, reachability root nodes, WeakMap/WeakSet.

explanation.overview: JavaScript engines automatically manage memory allocation and deallocation via Garbage Collection (GC), using the Mark-and-Sweep algorithm.

sections.heading: Mark-and-Sweep Algorithm
sections.content: Modern engines mark reachable objects starting from root nodes (global object, active call stack frames). Objects that cannot be reached by traversing references from roots are marked for collection.
bulletPoints: Roots: Global objects, active call stack local variables, active event listeners.
Mark Phase: Traverses reference tree from roots, marking reachable objects.
Sweep Phase: Unreachable unmarked objects are reclaimed from heap memory.

sections.heading: WeakMap & WeakSet
sections.content: WeakMap and WeakSet hold **weak** references to object keys. If an object exists as key ONLY inside a WeakMap, GC can reclaim it automatically.
bulletPoints: Non-enumerable: Cannot iterate keys because GC can reclaim items anytime.
Keys must be Objects or non-registered Symbols.
Prevents memory leaks in DOM metadata caching.

keyTakeaways: GC uses Mark-and-Sweep algorithm based on reachability from roots.
Reference counting was replaced due to circular reference bugs.
Use WeakMap/WeakSet to hold object references without preventing garbage collection.

codeExamples.title: WeakMap Garbage Collection Support
codeExamples.description: Demonstrating WeakMap holding weak reference to DOM elements.

mcqs.question: What primary algorithm do modern JS engines (V8, JavaScriptCore) use for Garbage Collection?
mcqs.explanation: Mark-and-Sweep algorithm determines reachability from root nodes, resolving circular reference leaks.

mcqs.question: Why was legacy Reference Counting garbage collection algorithm abandoned?
options: Could not reclaim circular references where two objects reference each other but are unreachable from roots
mcqs.explanation: Circular references caused reference counts never to reach 0, leaking memory indefinitely under reference counting.

mcqs.question: What defines an object as 'reachable' in Mark-and-Sweep GC?
options: It has at least one property
It is accessible via reference chain starting from global or call stack root nodes
It was created within last 5 minutes
It is stored in Local Storage
mcqs.explanation: Reachable objects can be navigated to via active references starting from root nodes.

mcqs.question: What unique garbage collection property do WeakMap keys possess?
options: Keys are held weakly; if no other references exist, object key and value can be garbage collected
mcqs.explanation: WeakMap references are weak, allowing GC to collect key objects when all external references are dropped.

mcqs.question: Can developers manually force immediate Garbage Collection in standard browser production JavaScript?
options: No, GC runs automatically controlled non-deterministically by engine heuristics
mcqs.explanation: Garbage collection in JS is non-deterministic and managed automatically by engine heuristics without production API.

title: Memory leaks
summary: Common causes of JS memory leaks: accidental global variables, uncleared timers/listeners, closure retains, detached DOM nodes.

explanation.overview: A memory leak occurs when allocated memory is no longer needed by application but fails to be reclaimed by garbage collector because unintended references persist.

sections.heading: 4 Primary Sources of JS Memory Leaks
sections.content:
1. **Accidental Global Variables**: Undeclared variables attach to `window` root.
2. **Forgotten Timers / Callbacks**: `setInterval` keeping callbacks alive.
3. **Detached DOM Elements**: JS objects referencing removed DOM nodes.
4. **Closure State Retainers**: Closures holding massive outer scopes.
bulletPoints: Globals: Never dereferenced until browser tab closes.
Timers: `setInterval` holds callback closure until `clearInterval()` is invoked.
Detached DOM: Retaining JS reference to element removed from document tree.

sections.heading: Detection & Prevention
sections.content: Use Chrome DevTools Memory tab (Heap Snapshots, Allocation Timelines) to detect leak retainers and memory growth trends over time.
bulletPoints: Always call `clearInterval()` / `removeEventListener()` on component unmount.
Nullify manual references to detached DOM elements.
Use strict mode `'use strict'` to throw error on accidental global assignments.

keyTakeaways: Always clean up timers and event listeners when components unmount.
Avoid accidental global variables by enabling strict mode.
Use Chrome DevTools Heap Snapshots to inspect memory leaks.

codeExamples.title: Memory Leak & Fix
codeExamples.description: Forgotten interval leak vs proper cleanup pattern.

mcqs.question: Why does an accidental global variable `foo = 'bar'` (without var/let/const) cause a memory leak?
options: It attaches to window global root node, staying reachable and un-collectable for lifespan of tab
It gets converted to a stream
mcqs.explanation: Global variables are properties of root node (`window`/`global`) which GC never reclaims while page is open.

mcqs.question: What is a 'Detached DOM node' memory leak?
options: A DOM node without CSS styles
A DOM element removed from page DOM tree but still referenced by a JavaScript variable
mcqs.explanation: If a DOM node is removed from document tree but a JS variable retains a reference to it, GC cannot free memory.

mcqs.question: What happens if `setInterval` is started inside a SPA component that gets unmounted without calling `clearInterval`?
options: Interval timer continues running in background, retaining closure variables in memory indefinitely
mcqs.explanation: `setInterval` callbacks remain active on event loop, preventing all variables referenced in callback closure from being collected.

mcqs.question: Which DevTools panel tab is used to record and compare memory Heap Snapshots to find leaks?
mcqs.explanation: The Memory tab allows taking heap snapshots and inspecting Retainers tree pointing to leaked objects.

mcqs.question: How can accidental global variable memory leaks be prevented automatically at language level?
mcqs.explanation: Strict mode `'use strict'` converts undeclared variable assignments into immediate ReferenceError exceptions.
